newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers begin final arguments in Megan's Law case.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers begin final arguments in Megan's Law case.

text.p: Final arguments begin on Wednesday in the trial of a New Jersey man charged with raping and murdering 7-year-old Megan Kanka, an attack that horrified a community and inspired Megan's Law for child molesters.

The prosecution charges that Jesse Timmedequas, 36, lured the girl into his Hamilton Township home to see a puppy on July 29, 1994. There he raped and strangled her, later dumping her body in a park two miles away. Prosecutors also introduced five statements in which Timmendequas admitted his acts.
The state is seeking the death penalty.
Defence lawyers called no witnesses after the prosecution completed its case on May 22 after 14 days of testimony.

The crime sparked a public outcry because the girl's parents, Maureen and Richard Kanka, had not known that Timmendequas, who lived across the street, was a sex offender twice convicted in assaults involving girls aged 7 and 5.

Megan's Law was the result of the family's impassioned campaigning. Originally it required sex offenders to register with authorities and empowered authorities to notify the public about those they regarded as posing the highest risk.

But a series of rulings left the state with the power to require registration but not to notify the public and that aspect of the law is being challenged in federal court. Critics say Megan's Law violates the Constitution by punishing criminals after they have served out their sentences.
Most other states now have similar laws and last year President Clinton signed a federal law making it easier for residents to get information about released sex offenders.

Testimony in Timmendequas' trial began in early May after almost three months for jury selection, complicated by the notoriety of the case and the law it engendered. Because of the publicity and defence arguments that Timmendequas could not get a fair trial, the jury of seven men and seven women was chosen from neighbouring Hunterdon County and are bused 20 miles each day to the courthouse.

Timmendequas was charged in an eight-count indictment, the stiffest charge of which was intentional death, which carries the possiblity of the death penalty. The other charges were kidnapping, aggravated sexual assault and felony murder.
